newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank keeps interest rates on hold.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank keeps interest rates on hold.

text.p: The Bundesbank said on Thursday its policy-making council left the German discount and Lombard rates unchanged at its regular meeting.

The German discount rate remains at 2.50 percent and the Lombard emergency financing rate at 4.50 percent. The central bank's main money market rate, the repo, was also held steady at three percent for the next two weeks.
The Bundesbank said it would set its next two repo tenders at a fixed rate of 3.00 percent, the rate that has prevailed since late August.

A Reuter survey of economists this week showed that none of the 10 polled expected any change in the central bank's credit policies and the German bond and share markets showed almost no response to the move.
Faint hopes of a cut in German interest rates were dashed on Wednesday when two leading members of the Bundesbank council said that interest rates were already at appropriate levels.
Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing, making an unusually categorical statement on monetary policy on Wednesday, said there was no reason to expect further cuts in German interest rates.
"Key rates are at a historic low here and nothing more is expected or necessary," Issing told German television.
Economists said the remarks came as no surprise given evidence of a stable recovery and low inflation.
Stable consumer price data from two German states, Hesse and Baden-Wuerttemberg, confirmed that inflation was well under control.
Both states announced on Thursday that consumer prices were unchanged month-on-month in October and up 1.3 percent year-on-year.

Bundesbank vice-president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum reinforced Issing's message, telling reporters early Wednesday evening that M3 money supply data, the central bank's main policy guide, indicated that interest rate levels are correct.
M3 money supply growth slowed to 8.4 percent in September from 8.7 percent, the latest steady move toward the top end of the Bundesbank's money supply corridor of four to seven percent.
